While this chapter presumes that judicial review is generally available 
and non-problematic, that presumption ignores both alternative remedies 
for violations of public law requirements and potential stumbling blocks to 
judicial review. Those latter preliminary objections to judicial review— 
questions of “reviewability,” “standing,” “ripeness,” and “exhaustion of 
administrative remedies”—^take center stage in Chapter 8.
2. THE COMPLICATIONS OF JUDICIAL REVIEW
Judicial review of administrative action exposes the tensions between 
two insistent demands: that the government respect the law and that the 
democratic branches, rather than the courts, run the government. 
Balancing these demands lies at the base of a series of questions that are 
raised by almost every instance of judicial review.
Hou) intensely should courts scrutinize administrative decision 
making'? Although only a small share of the decisions of federal 
administrators are actually tested in court, the ever-present possibility of 
judicial challenge significantly influences the path of pubhc 
administration. That the courts’ role is critical, however, does not render 
that role self-defining. If courts were to police agencies by assessing every 
administrative decision from scratch (de novo), any efficiency, expertise or 
other gains that Congress seeks by vesting authority in administrators 
might be nullified. Moreover, such a role would threaten to usurp policy 
authority from both Congress and the executive. On the other hand, a 
search only for some rational relationship between a dministrators’ actions 
and the goals of their empowering legislation would make the courts’ role 
almost superfluous.
As we shall see, the Adniinistrative Procedure Act makes 
administrative action with legal effect presumptively reviewable and 
submits administrators’ determinations to a wide range of potentially 
invalidating demands for proper conduct, both procedural and substantive. 
Not the least of these is the demand that administrative action be both 
reasoned and reasonable. But it is important to recognize at the outset that 
this presumption of reviewability (and its accompanying role for the courts) 
does not necessarily reflect the landscape of judicial review in the early 
Republic, where some agency action was unreviewable and other agency 
action was reviewable using solely a writ of mandamus or other 
extraordinary writ. That meant that, in certain areas, judicial review was 
significantly more limited than it is under modern practice and the APA.
